question: What is TypeScript and how does it relate to JavaScript?
answer:
TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript developed by Microsoft. Any valid JavaScript is valid TypeScript, but TypeScript adds optional static types, interfaces, generics, and other features on top.

TypeScript code is compiled (transpiled) down to plain JavaScript so it can run in any browser or runtime. The type system exists only at compile time and is erased from the emitted JavaScript, meaning types provide no runtime overhead.

question: What are the primitive types in TypeScript?
answer:
The core primitive types are string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, and undefined. These mirror JavaScript's primitive values.

let name: string = "Ada";
let age: number = 36;
let active: boolean = true;
let big: bigint = 100n;

Always use the lowercase forms (string, number) rather than the boxed object types (String, Number), which should be avoided.

question: What is the difference between a type alias and an interface?
answer:
Both can describe the shape of an object, and in many cases they are interchangeable. Key differences:

  • Interfaces support declaration merging (you can declare the same interface multiple times and they combine) and are typically preferred for public object/class contracts.
  • Type aliases are more flexible: they can represent unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and mapped/conditional types, which interfaces cannot.
interface User { id: number }
type ID = string | number;

question: What is the difference between any and unknown?
answer:
any disables type checking entirely; you can perform any operation on an any value and it propagates unsafely through your code.

unknown is the type-safe counterpart: you can assign anything to it, but you cannot use it until you narrow it with a type check or assertion. Prefer unknown over any when accepting arbitrary values.

let a: any = 5;
a.foo(); // no error, unsafe

let u: unknown = 5;
// u.foo(); // error
if (typeof u === "number") u.toFixed();

question: What does the never type represent?
answer:
never represents values that never occur. It is the return type of functions that always throw or never return (infinite loops), and the type of variables in unreachable code branches.

It is also the result of impossible type narrowing, which makes it useful for exhaustiveness checking in switch statements.

function fail(msg: string): never {
  throw new Error(msg);
}

question: What is the difference between never and void?
answer:
void means a function returns no useful value (it returns undefined) but it does complete normally. never means the function never returns at all, either because it always throws or loops forever.

function log(): void { console.log("hi"); }
function crash(): never { throw new Error(); }

So void is a normal completion with no value, while never means execution does not reach the end.

question: What is a union type?
answer:
A union type allows a value to be one of several types, written with the | operator. A value of a union type can hold any of the constituent types.

function format(id: string | number) {
  return id.toString();
}
format(42);
format("abc");

You can only access members that are common to all members of the union until you narrow the type.

question: What is an intersection type?
answer:
An intersection type combines multiple types into one using the & operator. The resulting type has all members of every combined type simultaneously.

interface Named { name: string }
interface Aged { age: number }
type Person = Named & Aged;

const p: Person = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };

Intersections are commonly used to merge multiple interfaces or mixins into a single composite type.

question: What are literal types in TypeScript?
answer:
Literal types restrict a value to a specific exact value rather than a general type. They can be string, number, or boolean literals.

type Direction = "up" | "down";
let d: Direction = "up"; // "left" would error

Combined with unions, literal types create powerful, self-documenting APIs where only a fixed set of values is allowed.

question: How do enums work in TypeScript?
answer:
An enum defines a named set of constants. By default enums are numeric, auto-incrementing from 0, but you can assign explicit values or use string enums.

enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } // 0,1,2
enum Status { Active = "ACTIVE", Off = "OFF" }

Numeric enums generate a reverse mapping at runtime. Many teams prefer const enum or plain union literal types to avoid emitting extra runtime code.

question: What is the difference between a regular enum and a const enum?
answer:
A regular enum generates a real JavaScript object at runtime, allowing reverse lookups and runtime iteration. A const enum is completely inlined at compile time, so no object is emitted and references are replaced with their literal values.

const enum Dir { Up, Down }
let x = Dir.Up; // compiles to: let x = 0;

const enum reduces bundle size but cannot be used in some isolated-module setups.

question: What are tuple types?
answer:
A tuple is an array with a fixed number of elements whose types are known at each position. Order and length matter.

let pair: [string, number] = ["age", 30];
pair[0].toUpperCase();
pair[1].toFixed();

Tuples support optional elements ([string, number?]), rest elements ([string, ...number[]]), and named labels for readability ([name: string, age: number]).

question: What are generics and why are they useful?
answer:
Generics let you write reusable components that work over a variety of types while preserving type information. A type parameter acts as a placeholder filled in when the function or class is used.

function identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}
const n = identity(5);     // T = number
const s = identity("hi"); // T = string

Without generics you'd lose type safety (using any) or duplicate code for each type.

question: What are generic constraints?
answer:
Generic constraints restrict what types a type parameter can accept, using the extends keyword. This lets you safely access known properties inside a generic function.

function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;
}
longest([1,2], [1,2,3]); // ok
// longest(1, 2);        // error: number has no length

question: How can you set a default value for a generic type parameter?
answer:
You can provide a default type after the parameter using =. If the caller doesn't specify or infer the type, the default is used.

interface Container<T = string> {
  value: T;
}
const a: Container = { value: "hi" };      // T = string
const b: Container<number> = { value: 1 }; // T = number

This is helpful for APIs where most consumers want a common default but advanced users can override.

question: What does the Partial<T> utility type do?
answer:
Partial<T> constructs a type with all properties of T set to optional. It is commonly used for update functions where only some fields are provided.

interface User { id: number; name: string }
function update(u: User, patch: Partial<User>) {
  return { ...u, ...patch };
}
update(user, { name: "New" });

question: What do the Pick<T, K> and Omit<T, K> utility types do?
answer:
Pick<T, K> creates a type by selecting a subset of keys K from T. Omit<T, K> does the opposite, creating a type with the specified keys removed.

interface User { id: number; name: string; password: string }
type PublicUser = Omit<User, "password">;
type NameOnly = Pick<User, "name">;

They are useful for deriving related types without redefining shapes.

question: What does the Record<K, T> utility type do?
answer:
Record<K, T> constructs an object type whose keys are of type K and values are of type T. It is ideal for dictionaries and lookup maps.

type Roles = Record<"admin" | "user", boolean>;
const perms: Roles = { admin: true, user: false };

type ScoreMap = Record<string, number>;

question: What do the Readonly<T> and Required<T> utility types do?
answer:
Readonly<T> makes all properties of T immutable (read-only), preventing reassignment after creation. Required<T> does the opposite of Partial, making all optional properties required.

interface Config { host?: string; port?: number }
type FullConfig = Required<Config>; // host & port required

const c: Readonly<{ x: number }> = { x: 1 };
// c.x = 2; // error

question: What do the Exclude<T, U> and Extract<T, U> utility types do?
answer:
Exclude<T, U> removes from union T all members that are assignable to U. Extract<T, U> keeps only the members assignable to U.

type T = "a" | "b" | "c";
type A = Exclude<T, "a">;  // "b" | "c"
type B = Extract<T, "a" | "z">; // "a"

They operate on union types and are built on conditional types internally.

question: What does the ReturnType<T> utility type do?
answer:
ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function type T. It uses the infer keyword internally.

function getUser() {
  return { id: 1, name: "Ada" };
}
type User = ReturnType<typeof getUser>;
// { id: number; name: string }

This is handy for keeping derived types in sync with the actual implementation rather than maintaining them separately.

question: What are mapped types?
answer:
Mapped types create new object types by iterating over the keys of an existing type and transforming each property. They use the [K in keyof T] syntax.

type Optional<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]?: T[K];
};
type Stringify<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: string;
};

Many built-in utility types like Partial and Readonly are implemented as mapped types.

question: What are mapping modifiers in mapped types?
answer:
Mapping modifiers add or remove readonly and ? (optional) during mapping. Prefix with + to add or - to remove.

type Mutable<T> = {
  -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};
type Concrete<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]-?: T[K];
};

Mutable strips readonly, and Concrete strips optionality from every property.

question: How does key remapping work in mapped types?
answer:
Since TypeScript 4.1 you can remap keys in a mapped type using an as clause, often combined with template literal types to rename keys.

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};
type P = Getters<{ name: string }>;
// { getName: () => string }

You can also remap a key to never to filter it out of the result.

question: What are conditional types?
answer:
Conditional types select one of two types based on a condition, using the form T extends U ? X : Y. They enable type-level branching logic.

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type A = IsString<"hi">; // true
type B = IsString<42>;   // false

When the checked type is a naked union, conditional types distribute over each member of the union.

question: What does the infer keyword do in conditional types?
answer:
infer declares a type variable inside a conditional type's extends clause to capture and extract a type from a larger structure.

type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T;
type A = ElementType<number[]>; // number

type Awaited2<T> = T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T;

It is the foundation of utility types like ReturnType and Parameters.

question: What is the keyof operator?
answer:
keyof produces a union of the property names (keys) of a given type as string/number literal types.

interface User { id: number; name: string }
type UserKeys = keyof User; // "id" | "name"

function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

It is essential for writing type-safe generic property accessors.

question: What is the typeof type operator in TypeScript?
answer:
In a type context, typeof captures the type of a variable or object, letting you reuse a value's inferred type without writing it out manually.

const config = { host: "localhost", port: 8080 };
type Config = typeof config;
// { host: string; port: number }

This differs from JavaScript's runtime typeof which returns a string. The type-level typeof is often combined with keyof.

question: What are indexed access types?
answer:
Indexed access types let you look up the type of a property using bracket notation at the type level: T[K].

interface User { id: number; name: string }
type IdType = User["id"];          // number
type Values = User[keyof User];    // number | string

You can also index array element types with number: MyArray[number] gives the element type.

question: What is type narrowing?
answer:
Type narrowing is the process by which TypeScript refines a broader type to a more specific one within a code branch, based on control flow analysis. Checks like typeof, instanceof, equality, and truthiness narrow the type.

function pad(x: string | number) {
  if (typeof x === "number") {
    return x.toFixed(2); // x is number here
  }
  return x.trim();       // x is string here
}

question: What is a user-defined type guard?
answer:
A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate (arg is Type). When it returns true, TypeScript narrows the argument to that type.

interface Cat { meow(): void }
function isCat(a: unknown): a is Cat {
  return typeof (a as Cat).meow === "function";
}
if (isCat(x)) x.meow();

question: How does the in operator narrow types?
answer:
The in operator narrows a union by checking whether a property exists on the object. TypeScript uses the presence of the property to select the matching union member.

type Fish = { swim: () => void };
type Bird = { fly: () => void };
function move(a: Fish | Bird) {
  if ("swim" in a) a.swim();
  else a.fly();
}

question: What is a discriminated (tagged) union?
answer:
A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common literal property (the discriminant) used to distinguish members. Narrowing on that property tells TypeScript exactly which member you have.

type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; r: number }
  | { kind: "square"; side: number };
function area(s: Shape) {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case "circle": return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
    case "square": return s.side ** 2;
  }
}

question: How do you implement exhaustiveness checking with never?
answer:
Assign the value to a never-typed variable in the default branch of a switch over a discriminated union. If you later add a new union member without handling it, the assignment will fail to compile.

function area(s: Shape) {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case "circle": return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
    case "square": return s.side ** 2;
    default:
      const _exhaustive: never = s;
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

question: What is structural typing?
answer:
TypeScript uses structural typing (duck typing): two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of their declared names or explicit inheritance. If an object has all required members of a type, it is assignable to that type.

interface Point { x: number; y: number }
const p = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };
const q: Point = p; // ok, extra props allowed via variable

This contrasts with nominal typing in languages like Java or C#.

question: What are function overloads?
answer:
Function overloads let you declare multiple call signatures for a single function, so the return type can depend on the argument types. You write several signatures followed by one implementation that satisfies all of them.

function reverse(s: string): string;
function reverse<T>(a: T[]): T[];
function reverse(x: any): any {
  return typeof x === "string"
    ? x.split("").reverse().join("")
    : x.slice().reverse();
}

The implementation signature itself is not callable from outside.

question: What are decorators in TypeScript?
answer:
Decorators are special declarations prefixed with @ that can be attached to classes, methods, accessors, properties, or parameters to modify or annotate them. They are functions invoked at definition time.

function sealed(ctor: Function) {
  Object.seal(ctor);
}
@sealed
class Greeter {}

They are heavily used by frameworks like Angular and NestJS. TypeScript 5 ships standard ECMAScript decorators; older code uses experimental decorators enabled via experimentalDecorators.

question: What are declaration files (.d.ts)?
answer:
Declaration files contain only type information with no implementation, describing the shape of existing JavaScript code so TypeScript can type-check it. They use the .d.ts extension.

// math.d.ts
export declare function add(a: number, b: number): number;

Many npm packages ship their own declarations; otherwise community types are available via the @types/* scope (DefinitelyTyped).

question: What is the difference between modules and namespaces?
answer:
Modules (ES modules) are file-based: each file with import/export is a module with its own scope, and they are the modern, recommended approach. Namespaces (formerly internal modules) group code under a named object within or across files using the namespace keyword.

namespace Geometry {
  export const pi = 3.14;
}
Geometry.pi;

Namespaces are mostly legacy now; prefer ES modules for new code.

question: What does the strict option in tsconfig do?
answer:
strict: true enables a family of strict type-checking flags at once, including noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, alwaysStrict, and others.

Turning it on gives the strongest safety guarantees and is strongly recommended for new projects. Individual flags can still be toggled off underneath the umbrella option if needed.

question: What does noImplicitAny do?
answer:
noImplicitAny raises an error whenever TypeScript would otherwise silently infer the any type for a value, such as an untyped function parameter. This forces you to be explicit and prevents accidental loss of type safety.

// with noImplicitAny:
function f(x) {} // Error: parameter 'x' implicitly has 'any'
function g(x: number) {} // ok

question: What does strictNullChecks do?
answer:
With strictNullChecks enabled, null and undefined are not assignable to other types unless explicitly included in the type. This prevents a large class of "cannot read property of undefined" runtime errors.

let s: string = null;        // error
let t: string | null = null; // ok
t.length;                    // error until narrowed

question: What are assertion functions?
answer:
An assertion function uses the asserts keyword to tell TypeScript that if the function returns normally, a condition holds; otherwise it throws. After the call, the compiler narrows the type.

function assertIsString(x: unknown): asserts x is string {
  if (typeof x !== "string") throw new Error();
}
function f(v: unknown) {
  assertIsString(v);
  v.toUpperCase(); // v is string here
}

question: What is the satisfies operator?
answer:
Introduced in TypeScript 4.9, satisfies checks that an expression conforms to a type without widening or changing its inferred type. You get validation plus the precise literal inference.

const config = {
  port: 8080,
  host: "localhost",
} satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
config.port.toFixed(); // still inferred as number

With a plain type annotation you'd lose the specific number type of port.

question: What are template literal types?
answer:
Template literal types build new string literal types by interpolating other types inside template-string syntax at the type level. They can combine unions to produce all permutations.

type Color = "red" | "blue";
type Shade = "light" | "dark";
type Theme = `${Shade}-${Color}`;
// "light-red" | "light-blue" | "dark-red" | "dark-blue"

TypeScript also provides intrinsic helpers like Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, and Uncapitalize.

question: What is the difference between type assertions (as) and type casting?
answer:
A type assertion with as tells the compiler to treat a value as a specific type without any runtime conversion or check. Unlike casting in other languages, it does not transform the value; it only affects compile-time checking.

const el = document.getElementById("x") as HTMLInputElement;
el.value;

Because assertions can be wrong, prefer type guards when you need real runtime verification.

question: What is the difference between unknown and any when used as a function parameter?
answer:
With any, the value bypasses all checks and any subsequent operation is allowed, infecting downstream code. With unknown, callers can still pass anything, but the function body must narrow the value before use, keeping it type-safe.

function safe(x: unknown) {
  if (typeof x === "string") return x.trim();
}

Prefer unknown for parsing JSON or handling external input.

question: What are optional and readonly properties?
answer:
An optional property, marked with ?, may be omitted. A readonly property can be set at creation but not reassigned afterward.

interface User {
  readonly id: number;
  name?: string;
}
const u: User = { id: 1 };
// u.id = 2;     // error: readonly
u.name = "Ada"; // ok

question: What is type widening and literal narrowing with const?
answer:
When you declare with let, TypeScript widens a literal to its base type because the variable is mutable. With const, the value cannot change, so TypeScript infers the narrow literal type.

let a = "hi";   // type: string
const b = "hi"; // type: "hi"

You can use a const assertion (as const) to force literal/readonly inference for object and array literals.

question: What does the as const assertion do?
answer:
as const tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, deeply readonly literal type for an expression. Object properties become readonly and literals keep their exact values rather than widening.

const point = { x: 1, y: 2 } as const;
// { readonly x: 1; readonly y: 2 }
const tuple = [1, 2] as const; // readonly [1, 2]

It is especially useful for deriving union types from arrays of literals.

question: How do distributive conditional types work, and how do you prevent distribution?
answer:
When the checked type in a conditional type is a naked type parameter that is a union, the conditional distributes over each union member individually.

type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type A = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]

To prevent distribution, wrap both sides in tuples: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y, which treats the union as a whole.

question: What is the difference between interface extends and intersection types for composition?
answer:
Both combine types, but they differ on conflicts. interface B extends A requires compatible members and reports an error on conflicting property types. An intersection silently combines them, and a property with incompatible types resolves to never.

interface A { x: number }
// interface B extends A { x: string } // error
type C = A & { x: string }; // x: never

Interfaces also benefit from caching and better error messages for object hierarchies.

question: How do you type a function that maps over a discriminated union to return a related type?
answer:
You can use a conditional or mapped type keyed by the discriminant to map each variant to its payload, often via an interface map and indexed access.

interface EventMap {
  click: { x: number; y: number };
  key: { code: string };
}
function on<K extends keyof EventMap>(
  type: K,
  handler: (e: EventMap[K]) => void
) {}
on("key", e => e.code); // e typed as { code: string }

question: What is declaration merging?
answer:
Declaration merging lets the compiler combine multiple declarations with the same name into a single definition. Interfaces with the same name merge their members, and namespaces can merge with functions, classes, or enums to add static members.

interface Box { width: number }
interface Box { height: number }
// Box now has width AND height

This is commonly used to augment third-party or global types.

question: How do you augment a global or module type in TypeScript?
answer:
Use declare global inside a module to extend global interfaces, or declare module to add to an existing module's types. This relies on declaration merging.

// add a property to Window
declare global {
  interface Window { appVersion: string }
}
export {};

The trailing export {} ensures the file is treated as a module so the augmentation is scoped correctly.
